title: A Cooler Route Home
section: 讲话 / 报道 / 讲座
transcript:
When cities publish maps showing where summer heat is most severe, they usually begin with satellite images. These images reveal the temperature of roofs, roads and other surfaces. They are useful for identifying broad patterns, but pedestrians experience heat in a different way. A stretch of pavement may appear hot from above while people on the street are protected by the shade of a building. A research group set out to see how often these two views led to different conclusions about a walking route.

The group selected pairs of routes that connected the same bus stop and residential area. Each route was roughly the same length. Volunteers carried portable sensors and followed the two routes within a few minutes of each other, swapping routes on the next trip so that a difference in walking speed would not consistently affect one route. They recorded air temperature, humidity and the amount of direct sunlight at street level.

On several afternoons, the route that looked cooler in the satellite image turned out to be the less comfortable one to walk. Its pavements were light in colour and reflected a good deal of sunlight towards pedestrians. On the other route, the darker road surface warmed up, but the pavement ran beneath a continuous line of trees. That shade mattered more to the volunteers than the temperature of the road beside them.

The researchers stressed that their results did not make satellite maps useless. The maps can narrow down where to investigate. But the team suggested that decisions about signs directing people to cooler walking routes should also use measurements made at pedestrian level. They had collected readings only on clear summer afternoons, so they planned to include cloudy days in a later trial.

questions.prompt: Why did the group question the use of satellite images alone?
options: Satellite images are taken only in the winter.
They miss the differences between pedestrians' experience and surface temperature.
They cannot show the location of urban roads.
Most cities cannot afford to analyse them.
questions.answer: They miss the differences between pedestrians' experience and surface temperature.
questions.explanation: 卫星图显示的是表面温度，行人却可能有建筑或树木遮阳，实际感受不同。

questions.prompt: Why did volunteers exchange routes on the next trip?
options: To test whether the sensors worked in different weather.
To let them compare routes of different lengths.
To reduce the influence of individual walking speed.
To measure afternoon and evening conditions separately.
questions.answer: To reduce the influence of individual walking speed.
questions.explanation: 交换路线能避免某位志愿者的步速持续影响同一条路线的数据。

questions.prompt: What made the route beside the darker road more comfortable?
options: Shade from a line of trees.
questions.answer: Shade from a line of trees.
questions.explanation: 尽管深色路面更热，连续树荫让行人在旁边的人行道上更舒适。

questions.prompt: What did the researchers recommend before choosing routes for cooler walking signs?
options: Selecting the route with the lightest pavement.
Including measurements made where people actually walk.
questions.answer: Including measurements made where people actually walk.
questions.explanation: 团队建议在用标志引导行人走较凉快的路线前，加入行人高度的实地测量。
